blocks.t: Stoichiometry is derived from Greek words: stoicheion (element) and metron (measure). It is the branch of chemistry that deals with the quantitative relationships between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation.
Laws Followed During Stoichiometric Calculations

items.title: Law of Conservation of Mass
items.body: — Mass can neither be created nor destroyed. Total mass of reactants = total mass of products in any balanced equation.

items.title: Law of Definite Proportions
items.body: — A pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same ratio by mass. E.g., CO₂ from burning wood, methane, or coal always has C:O ratio of 1:2.

blocks.head: Assumptions During Stoichiometric Calculations (From Notes)
items: i. No side reaction occurs.
ii. All reactants completely turn into products.
iii. Law of conservation of mass and law of definite proportions are obeyed.

blocks.t: The Mole

blocks.label: Mole (Book Definition)
blocks.text: The mole is the amount of a substance which contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 0.012 kg (12 g) of carbon-12. The elementary entities may be atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, and other particles.

blocks.label: Mole (Note Wording — Alternative)
blocks.text: Amount of substance having 6.02×10²³ of particles (entities) is called one mole. OR: Amount of substance having as many particles as present in 12g (0.012kg) of carbon is called one mole.

blocks.head: Represented by 'n' · Unit is 'mole'
items: 1 mole of ¹²C contains 6.02×10²³ atoms of ¹²C
1 mole of H₂O contains 6.02×10²³ molecules of H₂O
1 mole of NaCl contains 6.02×10²³ formula units of NaCl
1 mole of Na⁺ contains 6.02×10²³ ions of Na⁺

blocks.t: Molar Mass

blocks.label: Molar Mass (Note Wording)
blocks.text: Mass of substance (atom or ions or molecules or formula unit) in each mole called molar mass. Represented by 'M'. Unit is g/mol.

blocks.t: The molar mass is the sum of the masses of the component atoms.

Molar mass (M) = n × Atomic mass₁ + n × Atomic mass₂ ...

Example: H₂O = 2×1 + 1×16 = 18 g/mol
CaCO₃ = 1×40 + 1×12 + 3×16 = 40+12+48 = 100 g/mol
C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6×12 + 12×1 + 6×16 = 72+12+96 = 180 g/mol

blocks.head: Quick Mass Number Rule (From Notes)
items: Z (even) → A = 2×Z (except Be)
Z (odd) → A = 2×Z + 1 (except N)

blocks.t: Calculating Number of Moles

blocks.caption: Mole triangle — three routes to calculate moles: from mass (m/M), from volume (V/Vm), from particles (N/Nₐ)
blocks.alt: Triangle with moles at center, mass/molar mass on left, volume/molar volume on top, particles/Avogadro's number on right

blocks.t:
Moles (n) from mass:      n = m / M       → mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol)
Moles (n) from volume:    n = V / Vm      → volume (dm³) ÷ molar volume (22.4 dm³/mol)
Moles (n) from particles: n = N / Nₐ      → no. of particles ÷ 6.02×10²³

Rearranged:
  Mass           m = n × M
  Volume         V = n × Vm
  No. particles  N = n × 6.02×10²³
Types of Moles (From Notes — 4 types)

blocks.head: i. Moles of Atoms
items: 32g of S = 32/32 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ atoms of S
12g of C = 12/12 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ atoms of C
23g of Na = 23/23 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ atoms of Na

blocks.head: ii. Moles of Molecules
items: 18g of water (H₂O) = 18/18 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ molecules
44g of CO₂ = 44/44 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ molecules
180g of Glucose = 180/180 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ molecules

blocks.head: iii. Moles of Ionic Compounds
items: 58.5g of NaCl = 58.5/58.5 = 1 mole
100g of CaCl₂ = 100/100 = 1 mole

blocks.head: iv. Moles of Ions
items: Na⁺: 23g = 23/23 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ ions of Na⁺
SO₄²⁻: 96g = 96/96 = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ ions of SO₄²⁻

blocks.t: Sample Calculations (From Book)

SP 4.1: Moles of NaOH in 20g?
  n = m/M = 20/40 = 0.5 mol

SP 4.2: Mass of 0.5 mol HCl?
  m = n × M = 0.5 × 36.5 = 18.3 g

SP 4.3: Mass of 10⁻³ mol MgSO₄?
  M of MgSO₄ = 24 + 32 + 4(16) = 120 g/mol
  m = 10⁻³ × 120 = 0.12 g

items.q: Calculate the molar mass of KMnO₄.
Calculate the number of moles in 0.23 g of sodium.
Calculate the mass of 1.5 moles of Ca(OH)₂.
Given mass of KClO₃ is 24.5 g. Calculate its number of moles.
How many molecules are present in 1.75 g of H₂O₂?
items.ans:
M of H₂O₂ = 2(1) + 2(16) = 34 g/mol

n = 1.75/34 = 0.0515 mol

Molecules = n × Nₐ = 0.0515 × 6.02×10²³ = 3.1×10²² molecules

items.q: How many atoms are present in 15 g of a gold ring?

sections.title: Relationship between Mole, Molar Mass and Avogadro's Number

blocks.label: Avogadro's Number (Note Wording)
blocks.text: Number of particles in one mole of substance is called Avogadro's Number. Represented by Nₐ (after Amedo Avogadro). Unit is mol⁻¹. Value is 6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹ (exact: 6.02214179×10²³).

blocks.head: Key Property — Depends on Moles, NOT Molar Mass (From Notes)
items: If moles are similar, the number of particles will be similar — regardless of which substance.
Different masses of elements can have the same number of atoms if they represent 1 mole.

blocks.t:
1.0 g of H   = 1 mol = 6.02×10²³ atoms
23.0 g of Na = 1 mol = 6.02×10²³ atoms
238.0 g of U = 1 mol = 6.02×10²³ atoms

18.0 g of H₂O   = 1 mol = 6.02×10²³ molecules
180.0 g glucose  = 1 mol = 6.02×10²³ molecules

From notes:
4g of He   = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³
12g of C   = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³
32g of S   = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³
32g of O₂  = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³
64g of SO₂ = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³
58g of NaCl = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³
40g of Ca  = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³

blocks.head: Why Do Different Gases Have Same Volume at Same T and P?
blocks.body: Number of molecules or volume is moles dependent — NOT mass or molecular size dependent. If moles are similar → volume will be the same. If volume is the same → moles are the same → number of molecules is also the same.
blocks.note: This answers: 'Can 1 dm³ of H₂ and 1 dm³ of CO₂ have the same number of molecules?' → YES, if at same temperature and pressure.

blocks.t:
No. of moles = No. of particles / Avogadro's Number
  n = N / Nₐ

No. of particles = n × 6.02×10²³

SP 4.4: 3.76×10²⁴ molecules of glucose
  n = (3.76×10²⁴) / (6.02×10²³) = 6.25 moles

SP 4.5: Na atoms in 2.3 g sodium?
  n = 2.3/23 = 0.1 mol
  atoms = 0.1 × 6.02×10²³ = 6.02×10²² atoms

items.q: A copper wire contains 27.10×10²⁵ atoms of copper. Calculate number of moles.
Calculate molecules in 1×10⁻⁶ g of isopentyl acetate (C₇H₁₄O₂). Then find atoms of C, H, O.

blocks.label: Molar Volume (Note Wording)
blocks.text: Volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at given temperature and pressure is called molar volume. Represented by Vₘ. Unit is dm³/mol.

blocks.head: Two Standard Conditions (From Notes)
items: STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure): 0°C (or 273.16 K) and 1 atm → Vₘ = 22.414 dm³/mol (commonly rounded to 22.4 dm³/mol)
RTP (Room Temperature and Pressure): 25°C (or 298 K) and 1 atm → Vₘ = 24 dm³/mol

blocks.label: Avogadro's Law (Book)
blocks.text: Equal volumes of all ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

blocks.head: What This Means — Note Wording
items: If moles are similar → volume will be the same
If volume is the same → moles are also the same → no. of molecules also the same
22.4 dm³ of a gas at STP = molar mass in grams = 6.02×10²³ molecules = 1 mole

blocks.t:
22.4 dm³ of CO₂ at STP  = 44.0 g  = 6.02×10²³ molecules = 1 mol CO₂
22.4 dm³ of H₂ at STP   = 2.0 g   = 6.02×10²³ molecules = 1 mol H₂
22.4 dm³ of NH₃ at STP  = 17.0 g  = 6.02×10²³ molecules = 1 mol NH₃
22.4 dm³ of any gas at STP = molar mass in grams = 1 mol

From notes:
1 dm³ of H₂ = 1/22.414 = 2.68×10²² molecules
1 dm³ of CH₄  → same no. of molecules as 1 dm³ of H₂ at same T, P
1 dm³ of O₂   → same
1 dm³ of CO₂  → same

Formula: V = n × Vₘ

SP 4.7: Volume of 2.5 mol Cl₂ at STP?
  V = 2.5 × 22.4 = 56.0 dm³

SP 4.8: Volume of 4.75 mol CH₄ at STP?
  V = 4.75 × 22.4 = 106.4 dm³

items.q: What volume does 0.5 mol of O₂ occupy at STP?
How many moles are in 44.8 dm³ of N₂ at STP?
4g of He, 17g of NH₃, and 64g of SO₂ all occupy 22.414 dm³ at STP despite different masses and sizes. Explain.
items.ans:
All contain 1 mole of gas molecules.

4/4 = 1 mol He · 17/17 = 1 mol NH₃ · 64/64 = 1 mol SO₂

By Avogadro's Law, equal moles of ideal gases at same T and P occupy equal volumes (22.414 dm³ at STP). Volume is moles-dependent, NOT mass or molecular size dependent. Since all three are 1 mole, all occupy 22.414 dm³.

sections.title: Molar Mass and Density of Gases

blocks.label: Density (Note Wording)
blocks.text: Mass per unit volume called density. It is the lightness or heaviness of a substance. Density ∝ packing of particles. Represented by 'd' or 'ρ'. Unit: g/dm³ or g/litre.

blocks.t:
d = m/V  →  also written as  d = M/Vₘ  (for 1 mole of gas)

To calculate molar mass from density:
  m = d × V
  M = d × Vₘ = d × 22.4  (at STP)

SP 4.9: Gas with density 1.97 g/dm³ at STP. Find molar mass.
  M = d × Vₘ = 1.97 × 22.4 = 44.1 g/mol  → CO₂

blocks.head: Examples from Notes
items: Density of 49g of H₂SO₄ = 49/22.414 g/dm³
Density of 36.5g of HCl = 36.5/22.414 g/dm³
Mass of a gas with density 1.83 g/dm³: m = 1.83 × 22.414 = 41.02 g → molar mass = 41.02 g/mol

blocks.head: Why Density Depends on Molar Mass for Gases
blocks.body:
All gases at STP occupy the same molar volume (22.4 dm³). So density = mass/22.4 dm³. Higher molar mass → more mass in same volume → higher density.
E.g., CO₂ (M=44) is denser than H₂ (M=2).

items.q: Calculate the molar mass of a gas which has density of 1.34 g/dm³ at STP.
items.ans:
M = d × Vₘ = 1.34 × 22.4 = 30.0 g/mol

This matches NO (nitrogen monoxide): M = 14+16 = 30 g/mol.

blocks.label: Molar Concentration (Note Wording)
blocks.text: Moles per unit volume called molar concentration. Term used for solutions. Represented by 'C'. Unit: mol dm⁻³.

blocks.t:
C = n / V    (concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³)
n = C × V    (moles = concentration × volume)

Example from notes:
  0.25 moles dissolved in 1000 mL (1 dm³):
  C = 0.25/1 = 0.25 mol dm⁻³

  0.2 moles of glucose in 1 litre of water:
  C = 0.2/1 = 0.2 mol dm⁻³

SP 4.10: 27.64 g of K₂CO₃ in 1 dm³
  M of K₂CO₃ = 2(39) + 12 + 3(16) = 78+12+48 = 138 g/mol
  n = 27.64/138 = 0.2 mol
  C = 0.2/1 = 0.2 mol dm⁻³

blocks.head: Example from Notes — Sucrose
blocks.body: 171g of sucrose (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) in 2 dm³ of solution. M = 342 g/mol. n = 171/342 = 0.5 mol. C = 0.5/2 = 0.25 mol dm⁻³.

items.q: Calculate molar concentration of 7.9 g of KMnO₄ in 1 dm³. (M = 158 g/mol)
If 0.05 mol of NaOH is dissolved in 500 cm³ of solution, what is the molar concentration?

blocks.head: 7 Types of Stoichiometric Calculations (Notes — 7th type added)
items: 1. Mole — Mole
2. Mole — Mass
3. Mass — Mass
4. Volume — Volume
5. Mole — Volume
6. Mass — Volume
7. Mole — Particles (added from notes)

blocks.t: Steps to Do Stoichiometric Calculations (From Notes — 4 Steps)

blocks.caption: Stoichiometric calculation flowchart — 4 steps from given data to answer
blocks.alt: Flowchart: Step 1 write balanced equation → Step 2 convert known to moles → Step 3 compare moles of known vs unknown using equation ratio → Step 4 convert moles of unknown to mass/volume/particles

items.title: Moles of Known
items.body: — Convert given mass, volume, or no. of particles to moles using: n = m/M or n = V/Vₘ or n = N/Nₐ

items.title: Moles of Unknown
items.body: — Compare moles of reactants and product (known with unknown) using the balanced equation ratio. This gives moles of unknown.

items.title: Find Mass, Volume, etc.
items.body: — Use formula to convert moles of unknown: m = n×M or V = n×Vₘ or N = n×6.02×10²³

blocks.t: Reading a Balanced Equation — N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ Example

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)

i.   1 mol N₂ reacts with 3 mol H₂ to form 2 mol NH₃  (Mole interpretation)
ii.  1 molecule N₂ + 3 molecules H₂ → 2 molecules NH₃  (Particle interpretation)
iii. 22.4 dm³ N₂ + 67.2 dm³ H₂ → 44.8 dm³ NH₃  (Volume interpretation)
iv.  28 g N₂ + 6 g H₂ → 34 g NH₃  (Mass interpretation — check: 28+6=34 ✓)
Type 1 — Mole-Mole (SP 4.11)

Q: 3.3 mol N₂ reacts with H₂ → NH₃. How many mol H₂ consumed?
Equation: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃

1 mol N₂ requires H₂ = 3 mol
3.3 mol N₂ requires H₂ = 3 × 3.3 = 9.9 mol
Type 2 — Mass-Mass (SP 4.12)

Q: Mass of Al to react with 32.0 g Fe₂O₃?
2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s)

n of Fe₂O₃ = 32.0/159.6 = 0.02 mol
From equation: 1 mol Fe₂O₃ reacts with 2 mol Al
0.02 mol Fe₂O₃ needs Al = 2 × 0.02 = 0.04 mol
mass of Al = 0.04 × 27 = 1.08 g
Type 3 — Volume-Volume (SP 4.13)

Q: Volume of NH₃ from 100 dm³ H₂ (excess N₂) at STP?
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃

3 mol H₂ produces 2 mol NH₃  →  ratio = 2/3
V(NH₃) = (2/3) × 100 = 66.7 dm³
Type 4 — Mole-Mass (SP 4.14)

Q: Mass of Li₂CO₃ from 20.0 mol LiOH?
2LiOH(s) + CO₂(g) → Li₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(ℓ)

2 mol LiOH → 1 mol Li₂CO₃
20 mol LiOH → (1/2) × 20 = 10 mol Li₂CO₃
mass = 10 × 73.9 = 739.0 g
Type 5 — Mass-Mole (SP 4.15)

Q: Moles of HCl neutralized by 2.1 g NaHCO₃?
NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂

n(NaHCO₃) = 2.1/84 = 0.025 mol
Mole ratio HCl:NaHCO₃ = 1:1
∴ mol HCl = 0.025 mol
Type 6 — Mass-Volume (SP 4.16)

Q: Volume of H₂ at STP from 7.0 g Fe + excess H₂SO₄?
Fe(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

n(Fe) = 7.0/55.8 = 0.125 mol
1 mol Fe → 1 mol H₂
n(H₂) = 0.125 mol
V(H₂) = 0.125 × 22.4 = 2.8 dm³

items.q: CO₂ produced when 2.25 mol glucose combust? (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O)
items.ans:
Ratio glucose:CO₂ = 1:6

2.25 mol glucose → CO₂ = 6 × 2.25 = 13.5 mol CO₂

items.q: How much Fe from 160 g Fe₂O₃? (Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂)
items.ans:
n(Fe₂O₃) = 160/160 = 1 mol

1 mol Fe₂O₃ → 2 mol Fe

mass Fe = 2 × 56 = 112 g

items.q: Volume of CO₂ at STP when 4.5 dm³ of CH₄ burns? (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O)
items.ans:
Ratio CH₄:CO₂ = 1:1 (by volume at same T, P)

V(CO₂) = 4.5 dm³

items.q: Mass of NaOCl from 2.25 mol Cl₂? (2NaOH + Cl₂ → NaOCl + NaCl + H₂O)
items.ans:
1 mol Cl₂ → 1 mol NaOCl (ratio 1:1)

2.25 mol Cl₂ → 2.25 mol NaOCl

M(NaOCl) = 23 + 16 + 35.5 = 74.5 g/mol

mass = 2.25 × 74.5 = 167.6 g

blocks.label: Actual Yield (Book Definition)
blocks.text: The amount of the products obtained in a chemical reaction is called the actual yield of that reaction.

blocks.label: Theoretical Yield (Book Definition)
blocks.text: The amount of the products calculated from the balanced chemical equation represents the theoretical yield. It is the maximum amount of the product that can be produced by a given amount of a reactant, according to the balanced chemical equation.

blocks.head: Why Actual Yield < Theoretical Yield?
items: Processes like filtration, distillation, washing, drying, crystallization — if not properly carried out → decrease actual yield.
Some reactants may take part in competing side reactions → reduce desired product.
Reaction may be reversible → backward reaction reduces product.

blocks.t:
% Yield = (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100

Greater % yield → higher efficiency of reaction

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Sample Problem 4.20 (p.86)
blocks.wrong: Problem states actual yield = 3.15 g, but the solution uses 2.85 g in the % yield calculation (2.85/3.96 × 100 = 71.97%). Also the number of moles calculation shows '300 g / 138.12' (300 g of salicylic acid) instead of 3.00 g.
blocks.correct: The actual yield given in the problem (3.15 g) should be used. % yield = (3.15/3.96) × 100 = 79.5%. The moles of salicylic acid = 3.00/138.12 = 0.022 mol (3.00 g is correct, not 300 g).
blocks.reason: Two separate printing errors in Sample Problem 4.20. Use 3.15 g (given in problem) for actual yield → % yield = 79.5%, not 71.97%.

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Sample Problem 4.17 (p.82)
blocks.wrong: Problem title says '1.81 g of NH₃' but the solution uses '18.1 g of NH₃' giving moles = 18.1/17 = 1.06 mol.
blocks.correct: The correct given mass is 18.1 g of NH₃ (not 1.81 g). The solution working is correct with 18.1 g.
blocks.reason: Decimal point error in the problem title. Use 18.1 g as in the solution.

blocks.t:
SP 4.20 (Corrected): Aspirin synthesis
C₇H₆O₃ + C₄H₆O₃ → C₉H₈O₄ + CH₃COOH

n(salicylic acid) = 3.00/138.12 = 0.0217 mol  ← limiting reactant
n(acetic anhydride) = 6.00/163.93 = 0.0366 mol  ← excess

Theoretical yield of aspirin = 0.0217 mol × 180.16 = 3.91 g
Actual yield (from problem) = 3.15 g
% yield = (3.15/3.91) × 100 = 80.6%

[Book gives 71.97% using wrong actual yield of 2.85 g — this is the corrected answer]

items.q: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Actual yield of CaO = 2.5 kg when 4.5 kg limestone is roasted. What is % yield?
items.ans:
M(CaCO₃) = 100 g/mol · M(CaO) = 56 g/mol

n(CaCO₃) = 4500/100 = 45 mol

1 mol CaCO₃ → 1 mol CaO

Theoretical yield of CaO = 45 × 56 = 2520 g = 2.52 kg

% yield = (2.5/2.52) × 100 = 99.2%

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
opts: One mole of nitrogen gas contains Avogadro's number of molecules
One mole of ozone gas contains Avogadro's number of molecules
One mole of ozone contains Avogadro's number of O atoms
One mole of hydrogen gas contains Avogadro's number of molecules
mcqs.exp: O₃ is a molecule. 1 mole of O₃ contains Avogadro's number of O₃ MOLECULES, not O atoms. It would contain 3×Nₐ atoms of oxygen (since each O₃ molecule has 3 O atoms).

mcqs.q: Which one of the following has greatest mass?
mcqs.exp: Mass = n × M. 0.5 mol CO₂ = 0.5×44 = 22g. N₂ = 0.5×28 = 14g. NH₃ = 0.5×17 = 8.5g. He = 0.5×4 = 2g. CO₂ has the greatest mass.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following gases will have greatest volume at STP?
mcqs.exp: Volume ∝ moles. n(CO₂)=22/44=0.5. n(N₂O)=88/44=2. n(CO)=28/28=1. n(N₂)=28/28=1. N₂O has most moles → greatest volume (2×22.4=44.8 dm³).

mcqs.q: Which of the following contains same number of particles as present in 12 g of carbon?
mcqs.exp: 12g C = 1 mol = 6.02×10²³. 48g Mg = 48/24 = 2 mol atoms? No: 48g Mg = 2 mol → 2Nₐ. Wait: 48/24=2 mol, that's 2Nₐ. 28g Fe = 28/56 = 0.5 mol atoms. Hmm — 48g Mg = 2 moles but we need 1 mole = 6.02×10²³. Actually 24g Mg = 1 mole. So 48g Mg = 2 moles. None match exactly. Re-check: B says 48g Mg = 48/24 = 2 mol — that's 2Nₐ atoms, not same as Nₐ. The correct answer should be D: 40g CO₂? 40/44 ≠ 1. Actually MCQ IV answer in book exercise is (b) — 48g Mg = 2 moles, which is NOT the same. Board answer is B (48g Mg = 2 mol ≠ 1 mol). This appears to be a book MCQ error. The logically correct answer would require 24g Mg = 1 mol = Nₐ atoms. Write for board: answer B per book.

mcqs.q: Volume at STP of 22 g of CO₂ is same as that of:
mcqs.exp: 22g CO₂ = 22/44 = 0.5 mol → V = 0.5×22.4 = 11.2 dm³. 2g H₂ = 2/2 = 1 mol? No, 2g H₂ = 1 mol → 22.4 dm³. Hmm: 1g H₂ = 0.5 mol → 11.2 dm³. So answer is A: 1g H₂ would give 11.2 dm³. But the option says 2g — 2/2 = 1 mol = 22.4 dm³ ≠ 11.2 dm³. Board answer per book: A. Note possible book error in option A (should be 1g not 2g).

mcqs.q: 4.0 g of NaOH (M=40) contains same number of Na⁺ ions as present in:
mcqs.exp: 4g NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol → 0.1 mol Na⁺. Each compound contributes Na⁺: NaNO₃: 8.5/85 = 0.1 mol → 0.1 mol Na⁺. ✓ Na₂CO₃: 10.6/106 = 0.1 mol but has 2 Na⁺ per formula unit → 0.2 mol Na⁺. NaCl: 58.5/58.5 = 1 mol Na⁺ (too many). Answer: D (8.5g NaNO₃ = 0.1 mol Na⁺).

mcqs.q: A container holds 0.5 moles of ideal gas at STP. What is the volume in dm³?
A solution contains 4.0 g of NaOH (M=40) in 250 cm³. What is the molar concentration?
10.0 g of unknown solute in 250 cm³. Concentration = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Molar mass?
N₂ gas (M=28) has mass of 14.0 g. How many nitrogen atoms present?
mcqs.exp: n(N₂) = 14/28 = 0.5 mol molecules. Each N₂ has 2 N atoms. Total N atoms = 0.5 × 2 × 6.02×10²³ = 6.02×10²³ × 1 = 1.20×10²⁴ atoms? Wait: 0.5 × 2 = 1 mol N atoms = 6.02×10²³. Hmm, but answer C is 1.20×10²⁴. 0.5 mol N₂ = 1 mol N atoms = 6.02×10²³ atoms — answer B. Board answer per book: C. There may be a book error; logically answer is B (6.02×10²³ N atoms). Check: 14g N₂ = 0.5 mol N₂ = 1.0 mol N atoms = 6.02×10²³. Book answer C appears incorrect.

mcqs.q: A gas has density 1.43 g dm⁻³ at STP. What is its molar mass?
mcqs.exp: M = d × Vₘ = 1.43 × 22.4 = 32.0 g/mol → this is O₂ (M=32).

mcqs.q: A gas has density 1.96 g dm⁻³ at STP. What is its molecular mass?

sqs.q: How is the concept of mole derived from Avogadro's number?
sqs.a:
The mole is defined as the amount of substance containing as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 12g of carbon-12 — which is 6.02×10²³. This number is Avogadro's number (Nₐ).

Therefore, one mole of any substance = 6.02×10²³ particles. Avogadro's number gives the mole its quantitative meaning — it is the actual count of atoms/molecules in one mole of substance.

Relationship: n = N / Nₐ → moles = number of particles ÷ Avogadro's number.

sqs.q: Define: (a) Molar mass (b) Molar volume (c) Molar concentration.
sqs.a:
(a) Molar Mass (M): Mass of substance (atom, molecule, ion, or formula unit) in one mole, expressed in grams. Unit: g/mol. E.g., M of H₂O = 18 g/mol.

(b) Molar Volume (Vₘ): Volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at given T and P. At STP (0°C, 1 atm) Vₘ = 22.4 dm³/mol. At RTP (25°C, 1 atm) Vₘ = 24 dm³/mol.

(c) Molar Concentration (C): Number of moles of solute dissolved per dm³ of solution. C = n/V. Unit: mol dm⁻³.

sqs.q: What do you mean by molar volume of a gas? How is Avogadro's number related with molar volume?
sqs.a:
Molar volume: Volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at given temperature and pressure. At STP: Vₘ = 22.4 dm³/mol.

Relationship with Avogadro's number: By Avogadro's Law, equal volumes of gases at same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules. Since 1 mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 dm³, and 1 mole = Nₐ particles, therefore 22.4 dm³ of any ideal gas at STP always contains 6.02×10²³ molecules (Avogadro's number).

22.4 dm³ at STP = 1 mole = 6.02×10²³ molecules (for any ideal gas)

sqs.q: 39 g of potassium and 56 g of iron have equal number of atoms in them. Justify.
sqs.a:
Molar mass of K = 39 g/mol → 39g K = 39/39 = 1 mole of K atoms

Molar mass of Fe = 56 g/mol → 56g Fe = 56/56 = 1 mole of Fe atoms

Both contain 1 mole of atoms. Since 1 mole always contains Avogadro's number of atoms (6.02×10²³), both samples contain 6.02×10²³ atoms.

This illustrates: different masses of elements can contain the same number of atoms if those masses represent equal numbers of moles.

sqs.q: 4g He, 17g NH₃ and 64g SO₂ occupy 22.414 dm³ each at STP though their sizes and masses are very different. Explain.
sqs.a:
All three samples contain exactly 1 mole of gas:

  • 4g He ÷ 4 g/mol = 1 mol
  • 17g NH₃ ÷ 17 g/mol = 1 mol
  • 64g SO₂ ÷ 64 g/mol = 1 mol

By Avogadro's Law: equal volumes of all ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Equivalently: equal moles of ideal gases at the same T and P occupy equal volumes.

Since all three are 1 mole at STP, all occupy 22.414 dm³. The volume is moles-dependent, not mass or molecular size dependent.

sqs.q: Do 1 mole of H₂ and 1 mole of NH₃ at 0°C and 1 atm have Avogadro's number of particles?
sqs.a:
Yes, both contain Avogadro's number of particles (6.02×10²³ molecules).

By definition, one mole of any substance always contains 6.02×10²³ entities. Whether the substance is H₂ (small molecule, M=2) or NH₃ (larger molecule, M=17), one mole of each contains exactly Nₐ molecules.

Additionally, since both are 1 mole of gas at the same T (0°C) and P (1 atm), they also occupy the same volume (22.4 dm³) — confirming equal numbers of molecules by Avogadro's Law.

sqs.q: Differentiate theoretical and actual yields. How is percentage yield calculated?
sqs.a:
Theoretical Yield: The maximum amount of product calculated from the balanced chemical equation, assuming all reactants are completely converted to products with no losses. It is always calculated from stoichiometry.

Actual Yield: The actual amount of product experimentally obtained from a reaction. It is always less than or equal to the theoretical yield.

% Yield = (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100

Why actual < theoretical: Side reactions occur; some product is lost during separation/purification (filtration, distillation, crystallization); reaction may be reversible (backward reaction reduces product).

sqs.q: What factors are responsible for low yield of products in chemical reactions?
sqs.a:
• Side reactions: Reactants may form unwanted by-products, reducing the desired product.
  • Separation losses: Processes like filtration, distillation, crystallization — if not carefully done — reduce actual yield.
  • Reversible reactions: The backward reaction partially converts products back to reactants → equilibrium limits yield.
  • Incomplete reaction: If reaction does not go to completion, some reactants remain unreacted.
  • Transfer losses: Small amounts of product lost when transferred between containers.

sqs.q: Calculate number of molecules in 5.6 dm³ of CO₂ at STP.
What volume of O₂ at STP contains the same number of molecules as 11g of CO₂?
sqs.a:
n(CO₂) = 11/44 = 0.25 mol → 0.25 Nₐ molecules

For O₂ to have same number of molecules → need 0.25 mol O₂

V(O₂) = n × Vₘ = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³

sqs.q: What is % yield? Aspirin synthesis: theoretical yield = 3.91 g, actual = 3.15 g. Calculate % yield.
sqs.a:
% Yield = (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100

% yield = (3.15 / 3.91) × 100 = 80.6%

This means 80.6% of the maximum possible aspirin was actually obtained. Losses of 19.4% are due to side reactions, mechanical losses during filtration/drying, and reversible reactions.

quiz.q: Stoichiometry is derived from the Greek word 'metron' which means:
quiz.exp: Stoicheion = element, metron = measure. Stoichiometry literally means 'measuring elements'.

quiz.q: One mole of any substance contains:
quiz.exp: One mole always contains exactly 6.02×10²³ particles (Avogadro's number), regardless of the substance.

At STP, 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies:
quiz.exp: Molar volume at STP (0°C, 1 atm) = 22.4 dm³/mol for any ideal gas. At RTP (25°C) it is 24 dm³/mol.

In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of H₂ react with 2 mol N₂?
quiz.exp: Ratio N₂:H₂ = 1:3. So 2 mol N₂ needs 2×3 = 6 mol H₂.

quiz.q: Which law states total mass of reactants equals total mass of products?
quiz.exp: Law of conservation of mass: matter can neither be created nor destroyed. Total mass reactants = total mass products in a balanced equation.

quiz.q: By Avogadro's Law, equal volumes of gases at same T and P have equal:
quiz.exp: Avogadro's Law: equal volumes of ideal gases at same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

The actual yield is always _____ the theoretical yield.
quiz.exp: Actual yield ≤ theoretical yield due to side reactions, separation losses, and reversible reactions. Theoretical yield is the maximum possible.

quiz.q: % yield formula is:
quiz.exp: % Yield = (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100. A higher % yield means higher efficiency.

quiz.q: Mass of 0.5 mol of Ca(OH)₂ (M = 74 g/mol):
How many moles are in 6.02×10²⁴ molecules of CO₂?
The 4 steps to do stoichiometric calculations are in the order:
opts: Balanced equation → moles unknown → moles known → find mass
Balanced equation → moles known → moles unknown → find mass/volume
Find mass → balanced equation → moles → compare
Compare moles → balanced equation → find mass → moles
quiz.exp: Step 1: Write balanced equation. Step 2: Convert known to moles. Step 3: Use ratio to find moles of unknown. Step 4: Convert moles of unknown to mass/volume/particles.

quiz.q: Density of a gas at STP depends mainly on its:
quiz.exp: At STP, all gases occupy the same molar volume (22.4 dm³). So density = M/22.4. Higher molar mass → higher density. d = M/Vₘ.

quiz.q: Which assumption is made during stoichiometric calculations?
opts: Only some reactants convert to products
All reactants completely turn into products
Law of conservation of mass is ignored
quiz.exp: The basic assumptions are: (i) No side reaction occurs, (ii) All reactants completely turn into products, (iii) Laws of conservation of mass and definite proportions are obeyed.
